content: Dock3, also referred to as MOCA (Modifier of Cell Adhesion) and PBP (Presenilin-Binding Protein), is a large intracellular protein with a molecular weight of approximately 180 kDa. It plays a critical role in intracellular signaling pathways. Dock3 belongs to the DOCK-B subfamily of the DOCK family of guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs), which are responsible for activating small G proteins. Specifically, Dock3 activates the small G protein Rac. Dock3 was initially identified in a screen for proteins that bind to presenilin, a transmembrane protein that is mutated in cases of early-onset Alzheimer’s disease. Dock3 is predominantly expressed in neurons, particularly in the cerebral cortex and hippocampus. Dock3 is a member of the GEF protein class, which facilitates cellular signaling by activating small G proteins. In their inactive state, small G proteins are bound to guanosine diphosphate (GDP). Activation requires the release of GDP and the subsequent binding of guanosine triphosphate (GTP). GEFs, such as Dock3, promote this nucleotide exchange, thereby activating the G proteins. Dock3 shares a similar domain arrangement with Dock180, a member of the DOCK-A subfamily and a prototypical member of the DOCK family. Dock3 and Dock180 exhibit approximately 40% sequence similarity. The activity of Dock3 is thought to be regulated in a manner similar to Dock180, given their shared domain structure. Dock3 contains an N-terminal SH3 domain, which in Dock180 binds to ELMO, a family of adaptor proteins that enhance GEF activity and recruitment. Additionally, Dock3 has a C-terminal proline-rich region, which in Dock180 interacts with the adaptor protein CRK. However, the specific binding partners of Dock3 have not yet been fully characterized. Dock3’s GEF activity is specifically directed toward Rac1. It has not been shown to interact with Rac3, another Rac protein expressed in neuronal cells, likely due to Rac3’s localization in the perinuclear region. Interestingly, Rac1 and Rac3 appear to have distinct and opposing roles in neuronal cells. Dock3-mediated activation of Rac1 promotes cytoskeletal reorganization in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells, primary cortical neurons, and fibroblasts, leading to morphological changes. Dock3 has also been implicated in regulating neurite outgrowth and cell-cell adhesion in B103 and PC12 cells. The potential involvement of Dock3 in neurological disorders was first suggested by its interaction with presenilin, an enzyme involved in the production of beta-amyloid (Aβ). The accumulation of Aβ is a key pathological feature in Alzheimer’s disease. In brain samples from Alzheimer’s patients, Dock3 has been observed to redistribute and associate with neurofibrillary tangles. Furthermore, a mutation in Dock3 has been identified in a family exhibiting a phenotype resembling attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
